title: How do you write a UGC hook that isn't clickbait?
description: A UGC hook that is not clickbait makes one small promise the video can keep. Learn how to write it, test it against the footage and fix one that overreaches.
short_answer: A UGC hook stops being clickbait when it makes one specific promise that the rest of the video visibly keeps. Write the payoff first, then write a hook that points at it, and check that a viewer who watches to the end gets exactly what the opening line suggested, no bigger and no vaguer.

sections.heading: What makes a hook feel like clickbait?

blocks.text: A hook feels like clickbait when the opening promises more than the video delivers, so the viewer feels tricked by the end instead of rewarded.

The problem is the gap, not the energy. A bold [hook](/glossary/#hook) is fine if the video backs it up, and a quiet one can still mislead. Watch for three warning signs in your own drafts: a claim about everyone, such as a line saying every viewer needs this; a secret or shock that the video never reveals; and a result the product cannot honestly show on camera. The post on [hook and payoff](/blog/hook-payoff/) explains why a mismatch loses the viewer. This answer is about writing the line so the mismatch never happens.

sections.heading: Why should you write the payoff before the hook?

blocks.text: Write the payoff first because the hook is a promise, and you can only make an honest promise once you know what you are able to show.

items: Look at the brief and your footage plan, and find the single moment a viewer would screenshot. That moment is your [payoff](/glossary/#payoff).
Describe that moment in one plain sentence, such as the lid clicking shut and the bottle staying dry upside down in a bag.
Now write a hook that asks the question the payoff answers. If the payoff is a dry bag, the hook can be about a leaky bag.
Read the hook and the payoff out loud one after the other. If they sound like the same story, you are close.

blocks.text: Working this way keeps you inside what the product can show, which matters for brand work because the brief limits what you can claim. The guide on [writing a hook](/how-to-write-a-hook/) covers the openers themselves; use it once you know the payoff.

sections.heading: How do you test that the video keeps the hook's promise?

blocks.text: Test the promise by writing the hook as a question, then finding the exact line or shot in your script that answers it. If you cannot point to one, the hook overreaches.

table_rows: Can the camera show the thing the hook mentions
Change the hook to something you can film
Is the payoff as big as the hook makes it sound
Shrink the hook, not the payoff
Does the answer land before the viewer gives up
Move the payoff earlier or cut the setup
Does it speak about you, not about everyone
Rewrite it in the first person
Would the brand sign off on the claim
Ask the brand before you film it

blocks.text: Run the check on the finished edit too. Watch only the first line and the last shot, back to back. If a stranger would feel the second answers the first, the hook is honest.

sections.heading: What does an honest hook look like in a full script?

blocks.text: An honest hook names a real, small problem the creator has, and the video ends on a shot that shows how that problem went for them.

blocks.script_caption: Example script — written for this answer, for a reusable water bottle with a locking straw lid

script_beats.say: I stopped carrying water to work because every bottle I owned ended up soaking my notebook.
script_beats.do: Hold up a crinkled, water-stained notebook to the camera.

script_beats.say: So I wanted one test before I trusted a new one: upside down, in my bag, all morning.
script_beats.do: Fill the bottle at the sink and click the lid shut.

script_beats.say: The straw folds down and the lid locks over it.
script_beats.do: Close-up of the straw folding down and the lock sliding across.

script_beats.say: In it goes, upside down, next to the notebook I am fond of.
script_beats.do: Drop the bottle upside down into a bag beside a clean notebook.

script_beats.say: This is the bit I was nervous about.
script_beats.do: Cut to the same bag later, unzipping it slowly.

script_beats.say: Dry notebook, dry bag. That is the one I carry now, and it is linked.
script_beats.do: Lift the dry notebook out, then the bottle, and hold both to camera.

blocks.text: The hook promises one thing, a notebook that stays dry, and the close shows exactly that. It says nothing about every bag or every commute, only what this creator saw.

sections.heading: How do you fix a hook that promises too much?

blocks.text: Fix an overreaching hook by making it smaller and more personal, not by padding the video. Swap claims about everyone for one thing that happened to you.

items: Swap a universal claim for your own experience, so a line about what everyone gets wrong becomes what you kept getting wrong.
Replace a vague secret with the actual detail, so the viewer knows what they are waiting for.
Cut words like best, only and never unless the video proves them, because each one raises the bar for the payoff.
If the brand asks for a stronger line, offer two versions and let the brand choose, the way the answer on [hooks for ads](/blog/ugc-ad-hooks/) suggests testing options.

blocks.text: If a negative angle is tempting, the answer on [negative hooks a brand will approve](/blog/negative-hooks-ugc/) shows how to keep it honest. Then run the promise check again before you film.

hooks: I stopped carrying water to work because every bottle I owned ended up soaking my notebook.
